report:
### Conclusion
Contrary to your initial expectation, the medical evidence indicates that the answer is **yes**: offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) as an additional option consistently increases overall HIV testing uptake and test frequency.

### Evidence Behind the Findings
* **Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses:** Large-scale systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials show that offering HIV self-testing significantly increases testing uptake compared to relying solely on standard clinic-based testing services (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40621547/).
* **Global Health Policy Guidance:** The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends HIV self-testing as an additional strategy specifically because evidence demonstrates its ability to reach populations who might otherwise not get tested due to stigma, privacy concerns, or healthcare access barriers (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-CDS-HIV-19.36).
* **Increased Testing Frequency:** Evidence highlighted by the UK National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) demonstrates that providing self-testing kits increases the mean number of tests taken and boosts overall testing coverage among priority populations (https://evidence.nihr.ac.uk/alert/self-testing-kits-increase-overall-hiv-testing-uptake-in-men-who-have-sex-with-men/).

By lowering logistical, privacy, and social barriers, providing an additional self-testing option enables more individuals to learn their HIV status.
